title: The fig tree and the temple (Mark 11:1–25)
word: The fig tree and the temple
hook: the king on a donkey, a withered tree, and pray believing and forgive

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bartimaeus shouted louder, threw off his cloak, and followed Jesus on the way. Your line was what wilt thou. Who did you ask? The way he followed ends today, at the gates of Jerusalem. Day two hundred twenty-one.

Every Palm Sunday, Catholics walk into church waving palm branches, and a lot of kids think it's the fun Sunday. It starts here. Jesus sends two disciples to fetch a young donkey, a colt nobody has ever ridden. He rides it down into Jerusalem. People throw their cloaks on the road, and cut branches from the fields, and shout. It looks like a king arriving. Then, over the next day, he does two very strange things. He curses a fig tree. And he turns over tables in the Temple. Mark tells them woven together, on purpose.
screen: `PALM SUNDAY STARTS HERE.` → `A KING ON A YOUNG DONKEY.` → `A FIG TREE, AND THE TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: First, the shout. The crowd cries, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna, blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord." Hosanna comes from Hebrew, save us, please. It's a line from the psalms, and Catholics still sing it at every Mass, just before the Eucharistic prayer's great moment. A king, but on a donkey, not a war horse. Second, the fig tree. The next morning he's hungry, sees a fig tree in leaf, and finds nothing but leaves. Mark adds, strangely, that it wasn't the season for figs. Jesus says no one will eat fruit from it again. Third, the Temple. He walks into the Temple courts and drives out the sellers and overturns the money changers' tables, and says: "My house shall be called the house of prayer to all nations? But you have made it a den of thieves." He's quoting two prophets, Isaiah and Jeremiah. The next morning they pass the fig tree, and it's withered from the roots. This is a Mark sandwich: tree, Temple, tree. Many readers hear the tree as a sign, the way prophets acted out signs: all leaves, no fruit. Busy worship that forgets to pray. Fourth, what Jesus says about it all. Not a lesson in cursing. A lesson in prayer. Have faith in God, he says: whatever you ask in prayer, believe. And then, the line that ends today's reading: "when you shall stand to pray, forgive, if you have aught against any man; that your Father also, who is in heaven, may forgive you your sins." The house of prayer starts inside. Before you ask, let go.
screen: `HOSANNA: SAVE US, PLEASE.` · `LEAVES, AND NO FRUIT.` · `A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL NATIONS.` · `WHEN YOU STAND TO PRAY, FORGIVE.` · then, large: `MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED THE HOUSE OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive before you pray. Settle and breathe. Let one face come to mind, someone you're holding something against. Not the biggest wound you have; start smaller. Picture them. Notice what your body does. Then, if you can, loosen your grip, even a little. Forgiving doesn't mean saying it was fine. It means not carrying it into this moment. If you pray, after that, bring whatever you were going to ask. If you don't, just let the space it left be quiet. The bell holds the time.
The fig tree and the temple. A tree with only leaves, a house of prayer turned into a market, and a lesson that ends: forgive when you pray. Today's word.
screen: `THE FIG TREE AND THE TEMPLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: forgive, then pray. Today, before any prayer or any big ask of anyone, check whether you're holding something against someone, and set it down first. Day two hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics reenact the entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday with blessed palms and a procession, sing Hosanna in the Sanctus at every Mass, and exchange a sign of peace before Communion as a gesture of reconciliation.

original.note: Greek letters for the Hebrew hoshia na: save, please. from Psalm 117 [118].

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus lost his temper at a tree.
what it means: a prophet's sign, woven around the Temple: all leaves, no fruit. then a lesson on prayer that begins with forgiveness.
what a scholar hears: a Markan sandwich (tree, Temple, tree), and a Temple saying that joins Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11.
